agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Agent-relevant as a coordination layer rather than a callable service: installed and launched as a CLI, exposes a local web UI, and supports completion webhooks into Slack or CI. It drives other agents instead of being driven by them; no API or MCP server is documented for inbound control. Behaviourally testable — two npm commands and a demo mode that needs no agent CLIs installed.

hlido_opinion.headline: A local-only browser console that makes several real coding CLIs work as a team — a thoughtful orchestration layer we could not verify, maintained by one person.
hlido_opinion.body: Hlido's automated public-surface checks recorded no passes on this run even though the page rendered and was captured in full, so the score reflects what our checks could VERIFY, not a judgement that the product is weak. Read the score as low confidence pending a re-test, and the notes below as what the captured surface says about itself. The captured surface describes Hive as a browser UI for an agent 'hive' that runs entirely on your own machine: an orchestrator assigns work and real CLI agents — Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Qwen Code and others — each do their part in browser terminals. The design decision that stands out is that Hive holds no credentials of its own: it drives the CLIs you have already authenticated, so it needs no account and no API key. The documented division of labour is concrete rather than aspirational — one model writes while another reviews the diff, one writes tests while another fixes the reds — and the supporting pieces are the ones that decide whether multi-agent orchestration is usable at all: the task graph is a markdown file in your repository that can be edited and committed with declared dependencies, team memory carries workspace conventions into later assignments, and --resume reconnects through each CLI's native session or injects a written handoff brief when it cannot. The security posture is stated carefully: it listens on 127.0.0.1 only, remote phone access is off by default and end-to-end encrypted with the trust root on the desktop, no inbound ports are opened, and any paired device can be revoked. Two real constraints: it is maintained by a single developer with a modest star count, and it is BSL 1.1 rather than a standard open-source licence — both of which matter for anything load-bearing. The interface is also primarily Chinese.

tier_rationale: FADING (50) is a measurement verdict: all required public-surface checks failed on this run, so the install path, the agent roster, the local-only networking claim and the encryption model are all unconfirmed by us. The score states what we verified, which was nothing, and a re-test is queued. It is not lower because the captured page is specific, internally coherent, and makes claims a user can falsify in minutes with two npm commands.
what_it_does_well: Holds no credentials — drives CLIs the user has already authenticated, so there is no new account or key to trust
Division of labour is concrete (write/review, test/fix) rather than a generic 'multi-agent' claim
Task graph is a markdown file in the user's repo with declared dependencies — inspectable and git-trackable
--resume handles the real failure case: native session recovery, with a written handoff brief as fallback
Security posture is specific: 127.0.0.1 only, no inbound ports, remote off by default, revocable device pairing
Works with nine named CLI agents plus anything else runnable locally — no vendor lock-in
what_it_fails_at: All required public-surface checks failed on this run — nothing below is independently verified by us
Single maintainer and a modest star count: real bus-factor risk for an orchestration layer
BSL 1.1, not a standard open-source licence — check the terms before any commercial dependency
Interface and documentation are primarily Chinese, with limited English
Only useful if you already have several agent CLIs installed and authenticated
Some capabilities are labelled experimental (team spawn, workflows) with no stability guarantee
best_for: Developers who already run several agent CLIs and want them coordinated rather than used one at a time
Cross-model review workflows where one model critiques another's diff
Local-only setups where code must not leave the machine
not_recommended_for: Teams needing a vendor-supported orchestration platform
Commercial deployments that cannot accept BSL 1.1 terms
Users without existing agent CLI installations and credentials
Anyone requiring independent verification of the security claims before granting local reach
red_flags: All required public-surface checks failed on this run while the page rendered fully — the score reflects unverified claims, not measured weakness; a re-test is queued
Single-maintainer project under BSL 1.1 rather than a standard open-source licence — both material for anything load-bearing

compared_to.verdict_diff: CrewAI is a Python framework for building multi-agent systems from code. Hive orchestrates existing CLI agents through a browser UI with no code to write. CrewAI when you are building the agents; Hive when you already have them installed.

Claude Code is one of the nine agents Hive drives, not a competitor to it. The question is whether you want one strong agent or several coordinated — and Hive's own pitch is that cross-model review catches more than self-review.

OpenHands is a complete agent platform with its own runtime and a backing organisation. Hive is a thin local coordinator over CLIs you already trust, from a single maintainer. OpenHands for an operated platform; Hive to avoid introducing a new credential boundary.
